html:
Hollywood, a district of Los Angeles, has been the centre of the American film industry since the 1910s, and through it the world's most influential maker of movies. Its first permanent studio opened there in October 1911, when the Nestor Film Company moved in.

Early American films were made mainly around New York and New Jersey, near Thomas Edison, whose company controlled key patents and sued rival filmmakers. Southern California offered sun almost all year, cheap land, deserts, mountains, beaches and cities within reach, and distance from Edison's lawyers. Within a few years most of the industry had moved west.

The studio system followed. By the 1920s a handful of companies, among them Paramount, MGM, Warner Bros., Fox and Universal, made films on a factory model, with stars and writers on long contracts and their own chains of cinemas. Sound arrived in 1927, colour later. From the 1930s to the 1950s, the "golden age", Hollywood films dominated screens around the world.

A court ruling in 1948 forced the studios to sell their cinemas, and television drew away audiences. The industry adapted with big-budget epics, then with blockbusters from the 1970s and global franchises.

Hollywood spread American language, fashions and dreams worldwide, much like jazz and later McDonald's. It also faced rivals, from Indian cinema, which makes more films each year, to the film industries of Europe, Nigeria and Korea. Many of its founders were Jewish immigrants from Europe, part of the same great wave of migration that filled Ellis Island.
